Question: A subset \(B\) of the set of integers from \(1\) to \(100,\) inclusive, has the property that no two elements of \(B\) sum to \(125.\) What is the maximum possible number of elements in \(B?\)
Solution:
Each number has just one possible partner that would make a sum of \(125\). Group these partners together:
\[
(25,100),\ (26,99),\ \ldots,\ (62,63).
\]
The first entries run from \(25\) through \(62\), and the second entries run from \(100\) down through \(63\). Thus these \(62-25+1=38\) disjoint pairs contain every integer from \(25\) through \(100\) exactly once.

The set \(B\) can contain at most one number from each pair. The remaining \(24\) numbers, from \(1\) through \(24\), have partners larger than \(100\), so they impose no further restriction. Consequently,
\[
|B|\le38+24=62.
\]
This bound is attainable: take \(B=\{1,2,\ldots,62\}\). Its two largest distinct elements sum to \(62+61=123<125\), so no two elements sum to \(125\). Therefore the maximum is \(\boxed{62}\), choice \(\text{C}\).
